newsitem.title: FRANCE: French jobless rise shows outlook grim.
newsitem.headline: French jobless rise shows outlook grim.

text.p: French unemployment climbed again in September, hitting a new record and starkly highlighting a grim economic landscape which economists said was unlikely to improve any time soon.
The number of people unemployed rose by 27,700 or 0.9 percent to 3,112,800 in September, lifting the jobless rate to 12.6 percent from a revised 12.5 percent in August.

The increase was likely to tighten the screws on Prime Minister Alain Juppe's deeply unpopular conservative government, accused by opposition parties and trade unions of abandoning the fight against unemployment.
The opposition Socialist party said the jobless numbers were a "disastrous consequence of the restrictive economic policy pursued by the Juppe government".

Marc Blondel, head of the Force Ouvriere union which was at the centre of last year's crippling strike against the government's austerity plan, called on workers to "fight layoff programmes and plans to shed staff."

Economists said the higher unemployment was likely to cast a pall over consumer confidence, brake spending and make it even harder for the government to sell its austerity policies to a profoundly sceptical public.
"This is really bad," said Credit Commercial de France economist Valerie Plagnol. "The worry is that there's a risk of still further deterioration."
Consumer spending, which was up 2.6 percent in the third quarter, fell 1.5 percent in September and consumer confidence dropped again and neared a record low.
"We were banking on unemployment rising to the end of the year, but 0.9 percent is pretty high," said Jean-Louis Mourier, economist with Louis Dreyfus Finance.
"Even if there are signs of an embryonic recovery, it's not enough to help on unemployment. Fourth-quarter growth is going to stay pretty weak."
The government is counting on an economic recovery to help France reduce its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product and carry it into European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.

In a move seen as increasing chances EMU will start on time, the European Union on Thursday approved a French decision to use a controversial 37.5 billion franc ($7.3 billion) payment from state-owned telephone operator France Telecom to cut France's deficit.

The decision eased some worries about the January 1, 1999 launch of a single currency, but raised market fears that the decision to allow budgetary "window dressing" to meet EMU criteria could undermine the new currency's stability.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis called the announcement good news. "I was very satisfied with the decision," he said.
In another filip to the government, the Bank of France shaved a key interest rate on Thursday, a move justified by weak economic growth and currency stability, economists said.
The Bank said it was cutting its intervention rate to 3.20 percent from 3.25 percent. Economists said the cut was a highly cautious step which left room for further monetary easing.
Arthuis said he was happy over the rate cut and added he wanted the "lowest possible interest rates" in France.
Economists agreed a rate cut never hurts in difficult economic circumstances, but they said it would have little effect on the economy any time soon.

"It is in many ways a symbolic cut because it's true the macroeconomic impact of such a small rate cut is not going to be major," Societe Generale economist Michala Marcussen said. "Basically the Bank of France is signalling that they are doing what they can do." ($1=5.106 French Franc)
